Yeah, so I think this is one of the more important and underappreciated considerations when you're thinking about how fast things go after you get to the point of fully automating AI R&D.

The basic intuition is something like this: if full automation of an AI company happens relatively late, say after we've already scaled compute by many more orders of magnitude, and after we've already picked a lot of the low-hanging algorithmic fruit, then there's less headroom left. You're closer to whatever the practical limits are, both in terms of how much more compute you can build, since you've already taken a big chunk of the world's economy and chip production capacity, and in terms of how much algorithmic efficiency is left on the table. In that world, even once AIs are doing all the research, the gains from that automation might be more muted, because the remaining improvements are harder to find, and you can't just keep scaling hardware quickly.

Whereas if full automation happens earlier, at a lower level of compute, maybe because algorithmic progress turned out to be faster than expected or because the capability threshold for automating research is lower than people think, then there's potentially a lot more headroom. You've got a large amount of potential compute scaleup still available, you've got algorithmic improvements that humans just hadn't gotten around to yet, and now you have this huge pool of AI researchers who can work on them. So in that world, I think you'd expect a more explosive dynamic, where the software intelligence explosion has a lot of room to run before hitting diminishing returns.

There's a subtlety here, though, which is that earlier automation probably also correlates with some other things. If you get there earlier, it might be because returns to research effort are good, which itself makes a fast takeoff more likely. So these factors kind of compound. On the other hand, if you get there earlier with less compute, your AI workforce is smaller in absolute terms, because you can run fewer copies, so the initial speedup might be somewhat less dramatic than in a world where you've got a massive compute stockpile at the moment of automation.

Overall, my view is that the timing matters quite a bit, and earlier automation pushes toward faster and more dramatic takeoff, roughly because of headroom. I think people sometimes model the intelligence explosion as if it's independent of when it starts, and I don't think that's right. Where you are relative to the limits, on hardware, on algorithms, on how much of the economy you've already absorbed, really shapes how much progress you can get from automating research.

r001.rationale: The response says full automation could happen later, after compute has been scaled by many more orders of magnitude.

r002.rationale: The response says earlier automation at lower compute leaves more headroom; it does not claim that reaching human-level AI at higher training compute implies more subsequent headroom.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame this is: the question is basically, when you get to the point where AIs can fully automate an AI company — so, you know, you've got AIs that can do all of the work that the researchers and engineers at an AI company do, and do it at least as well — how much further can things go from there? And I think a big input into that is when it happens, because timing tells you something about how we got there.

So one way to think about it: if full automation happens really soon — like, say, within the next couple of years — then that probably means it happened with relatively modest additional compute and relatively modest algorithmic progress beyond where we are now. And that's suggestive that the current paradigm has a lot of juice in it, that scaling is working really well, and that we're probably not near any fundamental limits. So in that world I'd expect a lot of headroom. You get the AIs to be as good as the best humans at AI research, and then there's just an enormous amount of further progress available, because you got there cheaply, so to speak. The returns to further effort are probably still high.

Whereas if it takes a long time — if it takes, I don't know, 15 or 20 years to get to full automation — then that's some evidence that progress was slow, that we had to grind out a lot of improvements, that maybe compute scaling had slowed down a lot by the time we got there. And in that world, I think you'd expect less headroom. Like, the fact that it was hard to get to human-level suggests that getting substantially past human-level might also be hard. You've probably already picked a lot of the low-hanging fruit along the way.

Now, I want to be careful here, because it's not a clean relationship. There's a version of the long-timelines world where it takes a long time because we hit some bottleneck, and then once you get through that bottleneck things go really fast again. So it's not like the correlation is perfect. But as a rough heuristic, I think earlier full automation implies more headroom, and later full automation implies less.

And then the other thing I'd add is that timing interacts with how much compute is around. If full automation happens in a world where there's just a huge amount of compute available — which is more likely in the shorter-timelines, everything-is-working world, because people are investing massively — then once you have AIs doing AI research, they can run a lot of experiments, they can run a lot of copies of themselves, and that drives progress forward fast. Whereas if it happens later and compute growth has tapered off, there's less raw capacity to turn automated research into further capability gains.

So I guess my overall view is that the speed and the headroom are kind of correlated through this common cause, which is basically "how well is the current approach working?" If it's working really well, you get both early automation and a lot of room to keep going. If it's working less well, you get both later automation and a flatter trajectory afterwards.

r001.rationale: The response discusses later automation as evidence of slower progress and possibly tapered compute growth, but does not say it could occur at a substantially higher training-compute level.

r002.rationale: The response links greater headroom to reaching automation early with modest additional compute; it does not state that human-level AI reached with much higher training compute implies greater headroom.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is how far along you are when full automation happens. If you can automate basically all the work at an AI company with systems that are still substantially worse than the best human researchers, then there’s potentially a lot of headroom. You could improve those systems until they’re as good as the best humans, and then potentially go considerably beyond that. And automation itself could help you make those improvements faster.

Whereas if full automation only happens once you already have systems that are much better than humans at most of the relevant tasks, then some of that headroom has already been used up. Maybe the last things you automate are a few particularly difficult parts of research, and by that point you’ve already gotten a lot of the gains from automating everything else.

So I wouldn’t treat full automation as a fixed point where you necessarily get some particular amount of further progress. It matters what capabilities were required to get there, how much research was already automated beforehand, and what bottlenecks remain. You could have enormous amounts of automated research effort and still be limited by how quickly you can run experiments or get more compute.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts automation at weaker versus stronger capabilities, but does not mention later automation occurring at a substantially higher training-compute level.

r002.rationale: It says automating systems that are below the best humans could leave more headroom, but does not state that reaching human-level AI at much higher training compute implies greater subsequent progress.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is how far along you are when you get full automation. If you can fully automate an AI company relatively soon, while there are still lots of improvements you could make to algorithms and training, then you potentially have a lot of room for very rapid progress. You can put a huge amount of automated effort into finding those improvements, and then the improved systems can help you do research even faster.

Whereas if full automation only happens after you’ve already picked a lot of the low-hanging fruit, there might be much less headroom for that feedback loop. You could still make progress by building more compute, but that involves physical infrastructure and takes time.

One complication is that you don’t need full automation to get a lot of acceleration. You might already have automated most of the work, with humans handling a few remaining bottlenecks. In that case, crossing the threshold to full automation might not be a particularly dramatic event. So I’d want to know both how much room for improvement remains and how much acceleration you’ve already gotten before reaching that point.

r001.rationale: The response says later automation may allow more compute to be built, but does not explain that full automation could occur at a substantially higher training-compute level.

r002.rationale: It links remaining algorithm and training improvements to headroom, but does not state that human-level AI reached at much higher training compute would imply greater subsequent progress headroom.
